description:
FILED s466bc (Opus) while shipping #1037.  NOT A REGRESSION -- this is
ir-spec \xc2\xa79.3's documented boundary, measured here for the first time with a
number attached.

MEASURED: with #1037 shipped, perl-tests/state.t goes TRANSPILE-FAIL (0 rows)
-> PARTIAL 88 pass / 0 fail of 166 planned.  The 78-row shortfall is NOT the
refusal's own cost: the `given` sits at line 350 inside
`foreach my $spam (@spam) { ... }`, and `my @spam` at line 347 is a FILE-LEVEL
lexical, so the compiler wraps the whole remainder of the file in one `let` --
one top-level form.  A die anywhere in it costs every row after it.

The same is true of every drop.  ir-spec \xc2\xa79.3 states it ("the unit of the
decision is the statement; the unit of the LOSS is the enclosing top-level
form") and argues it is not a regression against perl, which is right: an
untrapped run-time die at file scope costs perl the whole remaining program
too.  What is NEW here is that PCL's file-level `my` promotion makes the
enclosing form MUCH bigger than perl's notion of "what runs after the die" for
a test harness -- perl-tests/*.t files trap nothing, so both lose the tail; but
a runner that loads FORM BY FORM with per-form recovery (which the sweep does)
recovers at the next form, and there is only ONE form here.

THE QUESTION THIS TASK EXISTS TO ASK: is a file-level `my` still worth one
whole-file `let`?  Two shapes that would each cut the loss:

 (a) split the file-level `let` at every top-level statement that CANNOT
     read a later declaration -- i.e. emit a chain of nested forms instead of
     one, so per-form recovery gets more than one chance.  Costs nothing at
     run time (the nesting is the same lexical structure); costs compile time
     and readability.
 (b) promote file-level `my` to cells (the identity promotion that #470 and
     Direction D already use for some names) whenever the file has a drop or
     a refusal in it, so the remainder is not nested at all.  Narrow, and
     keyed on exactly the thing that makes the difference.

NEITHER IS SCHEDULED.  Sizing first: count, over the drop census + the ruled
refusals, how many rows sit AFTER a die inside the same top-level form.
state.t alone is 78.  The measurement is cheap -- the sweep already reports
`shortfall` and `unrun` per file (task #993 I2), and `unrun` is very nearly
this number.

RELATED: #1037 (this shape's first instance), #343 / the announce->DIE flip,
ir-spec \xc2\xa79.3 and \xc2\xa79.3b.
subject: The DROP form and the REFUSAL form both stop the rest of the enclosing TOP-LEVEL form; for a file whose first statement is a file-level `my`, that is the rest of the file -- perl-tests/state.t keeps 88 of 166 rows for this reason alone
